one_liner: A grammar-driven DFA-table lexer generator for C++, claiming 2x flex's throughput at similar table size.
what_it_does: LRSTAR/DFA is a command-line code generator (like flex, or the lexer half of flex+bison): you write a grammar in its own `.grm`/`.lgr` format and run the `dfa` (or combined `lrstar`) executable to emit C++ source implementing a compressed-matrix DFA lexer, optionally paired with an LALR parser also generated by LRSTAR. It is not a library you link against; the generated tables are compiled directly into your project alongside a small hand-written runtime (Token/LEXER classes in code/lexer.h and lexer.cpp) that you copy in. Keywords and comments are folded into the grammar itself rather than handled as separate lexer passes.
how_it_is_fast: The core technique is a compressed-matrix DFA transition table: each input character does one table lookup to advance state, with no backtracking and no separate hash-table lookup for keywords (keyword literals are compiled into the same DFA as identifier matching). Comment skipping is also expressed as ordinary DFA transitions rather than a separate scanning routine. The tradeoff for compile-time size is table compression (an explicit 'minimize lexer-table size' /m option), which the author says keeps generation fast even for large keyword sets, unlike more aggressive table-based generators such as re2c.
when_to_use: Compiler-style grammar with a large keyword set (hundreds of keywords) where you want them recognized without a separate keyword hash lookup
Already comfortable with a flex-like 'grammar in, C++ lexer source out' workflow and want a claimed 2x throughput bump over flex at similar generated-lexer size
Want lexer-generation (build) time and generated table size to stay small, even if that costs a few percent of runtime speed versus re2c
Building on Windows (MSVC, 32- or 64-bit) or Linux (g++), willing to vendor generated C++ into the build rather than link a library
Want the lexer and an LALR parser generated from one coupled toolchain (LRSTAR proper) instead of stitching together separate lexer/parser generators
when_not_to_use: Need the fastest possible generated lexer: by the same author's own account, re2c-generated lexers are up to 10% faster than LRSTAR's DFA lexers
Grammar needs matching-parenthesis-style recursive constructs handled in the lexer -- the author found a PDA-based approach ~5x slower and says to push that into the parser grammar instead
Need macOS support: the author's own build docs say plainly, 'ON MAC OS X SYSTEMS: I don't know about this, sorry'

Want an actively maintained or widely adopted project: 0 GitHub stars, 0 forks, 0 open issues, and this GitHub copy is a third-party 'maintenance fork' whose recent commits are GitHub-linguist/language-detection tweaks, not functional changes

Need benchmark numbers you can independently verify: the only figures are first-party, with no stated compiler, flags, hardware, or benchmark corpus, and the upstream SourceForge page for the same project cites a different number ('80% faster than flex') for what appears to be the same claim

integration.min_toolchain: not documented as a specific standard; author reports building with GCC 4.6.1 (2014) and Visual Studio project files are checked in; code style predates modern C++ (raw pointers, static class members), no C++11+ features required
integration.platforms: Windows (x86/x64 via -Dx64), Linux (g++ with -DLINUX); macOS explicitly untested/unsupported per author
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the runtime LEXER class exposes only static members (a single global lexer/token state), which suggests it is not reentrant or thread-safe
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: same generate-C++-from-a-grammar workflow as flex, but a different grammar file format (.grm/.lgr instead of flex .l) and a different runtime API (LEXER::get_token() instead of yylex()), so porting from flex means rewriting the grammar and lexer call sites, not swapping a binary

gotchas: DFA lexers can't natively handle matching-parenthesis-style constructs; the author's PDA-based workaround measured ~5x slower, so that logic belongs in the parser grammar instead
GitHub shows this repo as having no license because there is no root LICENSE file, even though doc/software_license.txt and source_dfa/license.txt both state BSD-3-Clause
Generated LALR/DFA table files are marked read-only by the tool; the project's own setup notes warn to check your editor's read-only-file handling or regeneration can silently fail
Default build target is 32-bit; 64-bit executables require an explicit -Dx64 (Windows) or -Dx64 command-line flag
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LRSTAR/DFA over Ragel when you want a stated numeric improvement over flex (2x, even if first-party/unverified) rather than Ragel's directional-only 'faster than flex, slower than re2c' claim with no ratio; pick it over re2c-class or SIMD approaches (simd-lexing, StreamTok) when your grammar has a large keyword set and short lexer-generation time and small table size matter more to you than the last ~10% of runtime throughput.
verified_claims_summary: The only benchmark is a first-party statement on the project's own DFA documentation page: DFA-generated lexers are 'TWO TIMES the speed of "flex" created lexers and about the same size,' with no compiler, compiler flags, hardware, or benchmark corpus given. The same page states re2c-generated lexers are up to 10% faster than LRSTAR's DFA lexers, so LRSTAR is presented as beating flex but not re2c.
status_note: Listed as actively maintained (last commit 2026-04-19) and copyable (BSD-3-Clause, confirmed via doc/software_license.txt and source_dfa/license.txt despite GitHub showing no license), but this GitHub repository is a third-party 'maintenance fork' of Paul B Mann's SourceForge project and its recent commits are GitHub-linguist tweaks rather than functional work -- treat the SourceForge project as the canonical upstream.
